review_basis: Original SAP-C03 Module 01 high-resolution WebP slides 23–30 inspected separately; narrations trace their actual diagrams, comparisons, permissions and security caveats.
part_title: AWS Workload Identity — EKS, EC2, ECS, Lambda and Roles Anywhere

scenes.title: Amazon EKS Pod Identity
scenes.visual_overview: A pod's AWS SDK reaches its associated IAM role using the EKS Pod Identity Agent, EKS Auth and STS rather than embedded static keys.
visual_walkthrough: EKS cluster pod and Kubernetes service account on the left
Association maps namespace and service account to IAM role
Pod Identity Agent on the worker node exchanges a request with EKS Auth and STS
Temporary credentials return to the SDK for scoped S3 GetObject
Bottom compares Pod Identity with IRSA and shows trust and permissions policies
scenes.visual_example: The service account my-sa in my-namespace is associated with a role allowing s3:GetObject on an approved bucket prefix; the pod retrieves short-lived credentials through the node agent.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use dedicated pod roles, correct trust and restricted IAM permissions; weigh the platform support and differences from IRSA.
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates how an application inside Amazon EKS receives AWS permissions without a long-term access key. Begin in the left EKS cluster. The pod contains the application using the AWS SDK and a Kubernetes service account, shown as my-sa in my-namespace. Follow the association box at the top: EKS Pod Identity maps that namespace and service account to an IAM role. Next, the SDK requests credentials through the Pod Identity Agent running on the worker node. The agent works with the EKS Auth service and STS to obtain temporary role credentials and return them to the pod. The green S3 box on the right shows the resulting GetObject call, permitted only for the specified bucket or prefix. Notice the bottom comparison. Pod Identity uses an EKS association and node agent, whereas IRSA uses a cluster OIDC provider and web identity federation. The trust policy shown on the right allows the pods EKS service principal to assume the role, while the permissions policy limits what the pod can do. Platform support and workload compatibility must be checked rather than assuming all EKS environments use the same pattern. The key decision is to scope permissions to the workload and avoid placing static AWS keys in pods.

scenes.title: Workload identity on EC2, ECS and Lambda
scenes.visual_overview: Three columns compare temporary role credentials for EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles, and Lambda execution roles, highlighting the ECS task execution-role distinction.
visual_walkthrough: EC2 instance profile, IMDSv2 token and metadata credential retrieval
ECS task role for application SDK versus execution role for agent image pulls and logs
ECS container credential endpoint returns temporary credentials to container
Lambda service runtime supplies function execution-role credentials to SDK
Bottom never embed long-lived keys in AMIs, task images or environment variables
scenes.visual_example: An EC2 app reads S3 via instance profile; an ECS container writes DynamoDB using its task role, not the task execution role; a Lambda handler uses execution role credentials from its runtime.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The location where code executes decides the credential delivery method; always distinguish infrastructure roles from application roles.
scenes.narration: This slide compares how three AWS compute services supply credentials to application code. In the EC2 column on the left, an instance profile attaches an IAM role to the instance. The diagram follows the IMDS version two flow: the application obtains a metadata session token and then requests temporary credentials through the instance metadata service. No permanent access key needs to live inside the instance image. In the middle, ECS has two distinct roles. The task role is used by application code when it calls AWS APIs. The task execution role is used by the ECS infrastructure, for example to pull a container image and deliver logs. Follow the arrows from the container SDK to its credential endpoint and back. On the right, Lambda has a function execution role. Its managed runtime provides temporary credentials to function code, so the SDK can call the permitted AWS services. The bottom strip summarizes the choice: EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, and Lambda execution role. The common security principle is short-lived least-privilege credentials rather than long-term keys in images or configuration.

scenes.title: Temporary AWS access from outside AWS
scenes.visual_overview: An on-premises server uses an X.509 certificate and Roles Anywhere trust anchor and profile to obtain temporary credentials and scoped S3 access.
visual_walkthrough: On-premises workload with its certificate
X.509 certificate validation through configured trust anchor
IAM Roles Anywhere profile selecting the allowed IAM role
Temporary session credentials returned for AWS API use
Bottom calls out PKI rotation and revocation
scenes.visual_example: A datacenter service holds a certificate issued by an approved corporate CA and uses IAM Roles Anywhere to access a designated S3 bucket without storing a permanent IAM user access key.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Roles Anywhere is appropriate for certificate-based external workloads; credentials remain temporary and certificate lifecycle management remains essential.
scenes.narration: This architecture focuses on a workload running outside AWS, such as an on-premises server, that still needs AWS API access. Start on the left: the server has an X.509 certificate managed by the organization's PKI. Follow the arrow to certificate validation against the configured trust anchor. IAM Roles Anywhere uses that trust configuration and an associated profile, shown in the central green box, to select which IAM role may be used. The service then issues temporary role credentials, and the workload uses those credentials for narrowly scoped access, illustrated by the S3 bucket on the right. The bottom callout is important: owning a certificate is an operational responsibility. You need issuance, expiration, rotation, and appropriate revocation processes. A trustworthy certificate also does not bypass the IAM role's permissions. This pattern is useful when external servers need AWS access but storing long-lived IAM user keys is undesirable. It differs from OIDC federation, which uses trusted identity tokens rather than the certificate-based Roles Anywhere flow.

scenes.title: Hybrid and multi-cloud identity trade-offs
scenes.visual_overview: Four side-by-side identity patterns compare workforce, application users, on-premises servers and workloads in other clouds, each with a different federation and credential path.
visual_walkthrough: Corporate workforce directory federates to IAM Identity Center for AWS account access
Customers sign in through Cognito user pools for application tokens
On-premises server presents X.509 certificate to IAM Roles Anywhere for temporary AWS roles
Other-cloud workload uses a supported OIDC issuer and STS web identity exchange
Bottom trust questions: who authenticates, who issues credentials and what policies limit access
scenes.visual_example: For one enterprise, employees access accounts through Identity Center, customers authenticate to an app with Cognito, datacenter agents use certificates, and a supported other-cloud workload exchanges OIDC identity for AWS credentials.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Do not conflate source identity with authorization: evaluate the identity provider, credential issuer and effective IAM policy separately.
scenes.narration: This visual compares four identity architectures. They are alternatives for different actors, not four steps in one request. First, corporate employees use an enterprise directory and federation to IAM Identity Center, which assigns authorized access to AWS accounts. Second, customers using a web or mobile application authenticate through an identity service such as Cognito user pools, receiving application tokens. That path does not automatically provide AWS API credentials. Third, an on-premises server holding an X.509 certificate can use IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain temporary credentials for a permitted role. Fourth, a workload running in another cloud may use a supported OIDC identity provider and STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, with issuer, audience and subject constrained by IAM trust. Now examine the bottom three questions. Who authenticates the identity? Who issues the AWS credentials, if any? Which role and policies constrain what can be done? Those questions prevent a common design mistake: confusing application authentication with AWS resource authorization. Choose the pattern that matches the caller's environment and maintain least privilege and short-lived credentials wherever applicable.
